claim: Prostate cancer accounts for 20% of all newly diagnosed cancers in the United States.
source: Prostate cancer (PCa) accounts for 20% of all newly diagnosed cancers and is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in men in the United States (Siegel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2019

claim: Prostate cancer is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in men in the United States.
source: Prostate cancer (PCa) accounts for 20% of all newly diagnosed cancers and is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in men in the United States (Siegel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2019

claim: Many factors contribute to prostate cancer, including genetics, diet, age, and race.
source: Many factors contribute to PCa, including genetics, diet, age, and race (Gann, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gann, 2002

claim: Androgen receptor is considered the primary oncogenic driver for prostate cancer.
source: Androgen receptor (AR) is considered the primary oncogenic driver for PCa (Heinlein and Chang, 2004; Huggins and Hodges, 1941)
evidence: Supported by citations to Heinlein and Chang, 2004 and Huggins and Hodges, 1941

claim: Therapies targeting AR activity are current standard of care for metastatic prostate cancer.
source: therapies targeting AR activity are current standard of care, especially for those with metastatic PCa (Polotti et al., 2017; Virgo et al., 2017; Watson et al., 2015; Crawford et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Patients develop resistance to AR-targeting therapies with time and fail therapy.
source: Unfortunately, patients develop resistance with time and fail therapy (Watson et al., 2015; Bubley and Balk, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Watson et al., 2015 and Bubley and Balk, 2017

claim: The integrated stress response is critical for cell adaptation and survival to environmental stresses.
source: The integrated stress response (ISR) is critical for cell adaptation and survival to environmental stresses.
evidence: Draws from established scientific understanding of the ISR

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2α triggers reductions in global protein synthesis to conserve energy and nutrients.
source: Central to the ISR is phosphorylation of the α subunit of eIF2 (p-eIF2α), which triggers reductions in global protein synthesis to conserve energy and nutrients, and concomitantly facilitates adaptive gene expression (Baird and Wek, 2012; Tian et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baird and Wek, 2012 and Tian et al., 2021

claim: GCN2 is induced by amino acid starvation and conditions that trigger ribosomal collisions or stalling.
source: The eIF2α kinase GCN2 (EIF2AK4) is induced by amino acid starvation and other conditions that trigger ribosomal collisions or stalling (Dong et al., 2000; Inglis et al., 2019; Wek et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dong et al., 2000, Inglis et al., 2019, and Wek et al., 1995

claim: PERK is responsive to disruptions in the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: PERK (EIF2AK3) is responsive to disruptions in the endoplasmic reticulum (Walter and Ron, 2011; Wek and Cavener, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Walter and Ron, 2011 and Wek and Cavener, 2007

claim: PKR is activated by viral infection and inflammation.
source: PKR (EIF2AK2) is activated by viral infection and inflammation (Chukwurah et al., 2021; García et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to Chukwurah et al., 2021 and García et al., 2006

claim: HRI is enhanced by restricted heme or iron supply, oxidative stress, and disruptions in mitochondrial function.
source: HRI (EIF2AK1) is enhanced by restricted heme or iron supply, oxidative stress, and disruptions in mitochondrial function (Fessler et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2020; Suragani et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fessler et al., 2020, Guo et al., 2020, and Suragani et al., 2012

claim: ATF4 is a transcriptional regulator of genes involved in amino acid metabolism and proteostasis control, oxidative stress defenses, and feedback control of the ISR.
source: activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), a transcriptional regulator of genes involved in amino acid metabolism and proteostasis control, oxidative stress defenses, along with feedback control of the ISR (Harding et al., 1999; Young and Wek, 2016; Hinnebusch et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harding et al., 1999, Young and Wek, 2016, and Hinnebusch et al., 2016

claim: Targeted inhibition of ATF4 impedes progression of MYC-driven cancers.
source: Targeted inhibition of ATF4 impedes progression of MYC-driven cancers, emphasizing the important role of this ISR effector in tumor progression (Staschke and Wek, 2019; Tameire et al., 2019; Nguyen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Staschke and Wek, 2019, Tameire et al., 2019, and Nguyen et al., 2018

claim: Depletion of GCN2 in LNCaP cells significantly decreased proliferation.
source: only cells depleted for GCN2 or PKR showed a significant decrease in proliferation (Figure 1A, B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, B and supplementary materials

claim: GCN2 depletion lowered p-eIF2α levels and ATF4 expression in LNCaP cells.
source: Whereas GCN2 depletion lowered p-eIF2α levels and ATF4 expression, knockdown of PKR, HRI, or PERK had no effect on p-eIF2α and ATF4 protein levels (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Knockdown of PKR, HRI, or PERK had no effect on p-eIF2α and ATF4 protein levels in LNCaP cells.
source: Whereas GCN2 depletion lowered p-eIF2α levels and ATF4 expression, knockdown of PKR, HRI, or PERK had no effect on p-eIF2α and ATF4 protein levels (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Knockdown of GCN2 reduced growth in LAPC-4, C4-2B, MR49F, 22Rv1, and PC-3 cells.
source: In each of these PCa cell lines, depletion of GCN2 reduced proliferation and lowered ATF4 expression (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Deletion of GCN2 using CRISPR/Cas9 in 22Rv1 cells reduced p-eIF2α and ATF4 levels.
source: In 22Rv1 and PC-3 cells, we were also able to achieve a deletion of EIF2AK4 (GCN2) using CRISPR/Cas9, which reduced p-eIF2α and ATF4 levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: Reintroduction of GCN2 into GCN2 KO 22Rv1 cells rescued the slow growth phenotype and expression of ATF4 and ASNS.
source: Reintroduction of GCN2 into the GCN2 KO cells rescued the slow growth phenotype, and expression of ATF4 and its target gene ASNS (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and 2C

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of GCN2 with GCN2iB caused significant growth inhibition of LNCaP, C4-2B, 22Rv1, and PC-3 cells.
source: Using the inhibitory concentration range of 500 nM to 10 µM of GCN2iB, we determined that pharmacological inhibition of GCN2 also caused significant growth inhibition of LNCaP cells, and similarly reduced the growth of C4-2B, 22Rv1, and PC-3 cells (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A

claim: Treatment of LNCaP cells with GCN2iB lowered activation of GCN2, reduced p-eIF2α levels, and lowered expression of ATF4 and its target genes ASNS and TRIB3.
source: As expected, treatment of the LNCaP, 22Rv1, C4-2B, or PC-3 cells with GCN2iB lowered activation of GCN2 as measured by autophosphorylation of the activation loop (p-GCN2-T899), reduced p-eIF2α levels, and lowered expression of ATF4, and its target genes ASNS and TRIB3.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C

claim: Depletion of ATF4 using siRNA in LNCaP, MR49F, C4-2B, and PC-3 cells reduced growth.
source: To further test the importance of the ISR in PCa, we selectively depleted ATF4 using siRNA in LNCaP, MR49F, C4-2B, and PC-3 cells and observed similar growth inhibition for each cell line (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 4, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: GCN2 is not active in the non-cancerous prostate epithelial cell line BPH-1.
source: Importantly, GCN2 is not active in the non-cancerous prostate epithelial cell line BPH-1 (Hayward et al., 1995)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and citation to Hayward et al., 1995

claim: Loss of GCN2 or ATF4, or pharmacological inhibition of GCN2, did not significantly impact the growth of BPH-1 cells.
source: loss of GCN2 or ATF4, or pharmacological inhibition of GCN2, did not reduce p-eIF2α or ATF4 levels, or significantly impact the growth of these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, Figure 1—figure supplement 5B, Figure 1—figure supplement 5C, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5

claim: There was enhanced GCN2 activity in malignant prostate tumor samples compared to normal tissues as measured by p-GCN2-T899 staining.
source: Using immunohistochemistry and prostate tumor microarrays featuring normal and non-malignant prostate tissue (N = 33) and malignant tumor tissues (N = 88), we determined that there was enhanced GCN2 activity in the tumor samples compared to normal tissues as measured by p-GCN2-T899 staining (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Increased p-GCN2 (Thr-899) staining was observed in prostate tumors from patient core needle biopsies compared to adjacent non-malignant tissue.
source: In addition, increased p-GCN2 (Thr-899) staining was also observed in prostate tumors from patient core needle biopsies as compared to adjacent non-malignant tissue (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6

claim: Treatment of LNCaP cells with GCN2iB for 24 hr resulted in 239 transcripts showing a significant ≥twofold increase and 374 transcripts showing a ≥twofold decrease.
source: With 24 hr of GCN2iB treatment, 239 transcripts showed a significant ≥twofold increase, whereas 374 transcripts were decreased ≥twofold (fdr ≤0.05) compared to vehicle-treated cells (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Gene groups showing significant dependence on GCN2 for expression included those linked to amino acid deprivation and transport.
source: Included among the functional gene groups showing significant dependence on GCN2 for expression were those linked to amino acid deprivation and transport (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2B, C

claim: Of the 61 known SLC genes involved in the transport of amino acids, 27 were measurably expressed in LNCaP cells, and 20 of these were significantly decreased following treatment with GCN2iB.
source: It is noteworthy that of the 61 known SLC genes involved in the transport of amino acids, 27 were measurably expressed in LNCaP cells, and 20 of these expressed transcripts were significantly decreased following treatment with GCN2iB (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 2

claim: Treatment of LNCaP cells with GCN2iB lowered protein levels of xCT (SLC7A11), CAT-1 (SLC7A1), ASCT1 (SLC1A4), ASCT2 (SLC1A5), and 4F2 (SLC3A2).
source: xCT (SLC7A11), CAT-1 (SLC7A1), ASCT1 (SLC1A4), ASCT2 (SLC1A5), and 4F2 (SLC3A2) protein levels were sharply lowered with GCN2iB treatment of LNCaP cells, along with reduced expression of ATF4 and its target gene ASNS (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Treatment of C4-2B, 22Rv1, and PC-3 cells with GCN2iB reduced LAT-1 (SLC7A5), xCT (SLC7A11), and 4F2 (SLC3A2).
source: Similarly, treatment of C4-2B, 22Rv1, and PC-3 cells with GCN2iB also reduced LAT-1 (SLC7A5), xCT (SLC7A11), and 4F2 (SLC3A2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C

claim: Deletion of GCN2 in 22Rv1 and PC-3 cells diminished protein levels of xCT (SLC7A11), LAT-1 (SLC7A5), and 4F2 (SLC3A2).
source: We also measured transporter proteins in 22Rv1 and PC-3 cells and showed that deletion of EIF2AK4 (GCN2) also diminished protein levels of xCT (SLC7A11), LAT-1 (SLC7A5) (LAT1), and 4F2 (SLC3A2) (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Reintroduction of GCN2 fully restored expression of ATF4 and ASNS and partially restored expression of xCT (SLC7A11), LAT-1 (SLC7A5), and 4F2 (SLC3A2) in 22Rv1 cells.
source: Furthermore, the reintroduction of GCN2 fully restored expression of ATF4 and ASNS and partially restored expression of all three SLC proteins in 22Rv1 cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Treatment of LNCaP cells with GCN2iB or deletion of GCN2 in 22Rv1 cells significantly lowered the uptake of leucine, lysine, and arginine.
source: Treatment of LNCaP cells with GCN2iB or deletion of GCN2 in 22Rv1 cells significantly lowered the uptake of each of these amino acids (Figure 2F, G)
evidence: Supported by amino acid uptake measurements shown in Figure 2F, G

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of GCN2 in LNCaP cells resulted in a sharp reduction in the amounts of essential amino acids including histidine, branched-chain amino acids, threonine, phenylalanine, and methionine.
source: With pharmacological inhibition of GCN2, there was a sharp reduction in the amounts of essential amino acids (EAA), including histidine, the branched-chain amino acids, threonine, phenylalanine, and methionine, and non-essential amino acids (NEAA), such as glutamate and glutamine, aspartate, asparagine, alanine, and tyrosine (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by amino acid measurements shown in Figure 3A

claim: Supplementation of additional EAAs into the medium reversed the proliferation defect caused by GCN2iB treatment in LNCaP cells.
source: While GCN2iB treatment of LNCaP cells cultured in standard medium markedly reduced growth, supplementation of additional EAAs into the medium reversed this proliferation defect and increased free amino acid pools in treated cells (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Supplementation with additional NEAA did not suppress the LNCaP growth defect triggered by GCN2iB treatment.
source: By contrast, supplementation with additional NEAA did not suppress the LNCaP growth defect triggered by GCN2iB treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Inhibition of GCN2 in LNCaP cells caused an increase in the G1 phase of the cell cycle concomitant with a reduction in S phase.
source: Both methods of GCN2 depletion caused an increase in the G1 phase of the cell cycle concomitant with a reduction in S phase, indicative of checkpoint control of the cell cycle that can occur with amino acid depletion (Lehman et al., 2015; Leung-Pineda et al., 2004; Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 3C and citations to Lehman et al., 2015 and Leung-Pineda et al., 2004

claim: Supplementation of LNCaP cells with EAA reversed the accumulation of cells in G1 phase elicited by GCN2iB.
source: Supplementation of LNCaP cells with EAA reversed the accumulation of cells in G1 phase elicited by GCN2iB (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 3C

claim: There was a reduction of aminoacylated tRNAHis upon GCN2iB treatment in LNCaP cells that was restored when additional EAA were supplemented to the growth medium.
source: There was a reduction of aminoacylated tRNAHis upon GCN2iB treatment that was restored when additional EAA were supplemented to the growth medium (Figure 3D, E, and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by CHARGE-seq data shown in Figure 3D, E

claim: Only the addition of histidine to the culture medium reversed the growth inhibition triggered by GCN2iB in LNCaP cells.
source: In alignment with our charged tRNAHis measurements, only the addition of histidine to the culture medium reversed the growth inhibition triggered by GCN2iB (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3F

claim: Removal of histidine from the growth medium increased G1 accumulation similar to GCN2iB treatment in LNCaP cells.
source: Removal of histidine from the growth medium increased G1 accumulation similar to GCN2iB treatment, while supplementation of additional histidine to the medium alleviated the cell cycle arrest triggered by GCN2iB treatment (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Supplementation with histidine alleviated the cell cycle arrest triggered by GCN2iB treatment in LNCaP cells.
source: Removal of histidine from the growth medium increased G1 accumulation similar to GCN2iB treatment, while supplementation of additional histidine to the medium alleviated the cell cycle arrest triggered by GCN2iB treatment (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Supplementation with the full complement of EAA or histidine alone significantly lowered p-GCN2, p-eIF2α, and ATF4 expression in LNCaP cells.
source: Finally, supplementation with the full complement of EAA or histidine alone significantly lowered p-GCN2, p-eIF2α, and ATF4 expression, although it is noted that histidine supplementation rendered only partial suppression of the ISR compared to addition of EAA (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3H

claim: Addition of EAA or histidine alone suppressed the slow growth phenotype of MR49F cells treated with GCN2iB.
source: Addition of EAA or histidine alone also suppressed the slow growth phenotype of MR49F cells treated with GCN2iB (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A

claim: In 22Rv1 cells, EAA or lysine alleviated the slow growth associated with deletion of GCN2.
source: However, in 22Rv1 cells, EAA or lysine alleviated the slow growth associated with deletion of EIF2AK4 (GCN2) (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: Supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5B

claim: A collection of SLC genes showed significantly diminished growth in LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells in a CRISPR/Cas9 screen, including LAT1 (SLC7A5), SLC25A36, SLC25A46, SLC27A1, SLC35A2, and 4F2 (SLC3A2).
source: A collection of SLC genes showed significantly diminished growth, including several that require GCN2 for expression, such as LAT1 (SLC7A5), SLC25A36, SLC25A46, SLC27A1, SLC35A2, and 4F2 (SLC3A2) (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 4A

claim: SLC27A1 and 4F2 (SLC3A2) were required for efficient growth of both LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells.
source: SLC27A1 and 4F2 (SLC3A2) were required for efficient growth of both LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Treatment of LNCaP cells with GCN2iB for 6 or 24 hr resulted in a reduction in GCN2 activation and lowered ATF4 mRNA and protein.
source: Treatment of LNCaP cells with the GCN2iB for 6 or 24 hr resulted in a reduction in GCN2 activation, as shown by p-GCN2, and lowered ATF4 mRNA and protein.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A

claim: Levels of 4F2 (SLC3A2) protein and mRNA were lowered with inhibition of GCN2 in LNCaP cells after 24 hr of treatment.
source: Levels of 4F2 (SLC3A2) protein and mRNA were also lowered with inhibition of GCN2, although this reduction occurred after 24 hr of treatment (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A

claim: Addition of histidine to the growth media of LNCaP cells reduced GCN2 activation and lowered expression of ATF4 and 4F2 (SLC3A2) protein and mRNA.
source: Consistent with our findings that histidine limitation in part drives GCN2 activation in LNCaP cells, addition of histidine to the growth media of LNCaP cells in culture reduced GCN2 activation and lowered expression of ATF4 and 4F2 (SLC3A2) protein and mRNA, while removing histidine from the media further increased GCN2 activation and expression of ATF4 and 4F2 (SLC3A2) (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B

claim: Removing histidine from the media further increased GCN2 activation and expression of ATF4 and 4F2 (SLC3A2) in LNCaP cells.
source: addition of histidine to the growth media of LNCaP cells in culture reduced GCN2 activation and lowered expression of ATF4 and 4F2 (SLC3A2) protein and mRNA, while removing histidine from the media further increased GCN2 activation and expression of ATF4 and 4F2 (SLC3A2) (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B

claim: Addition of salubrinal alone increased 4F2 (SLC3A2) expression and also restored 4F2 (SLC3A2) expression in cells treated with GCN2iB.
source: Supporting the idea that p-eIF2α is critical for 4F2 (SLC3A2) expression, addition of salubrinal alone increased 4F2 (SLC3A2) expression and also restored 4F2 (SLC3A2) expression in cells treated with GCN2iB (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A

claim: Overexpression of GADD34 reduced phosphorylation of eIF2α and expression of ATF4 and 4F2 (SLC3A2).
source: In addition, overexpression of the PP1-targeting protein GADD34 (Novoa et al., 2001) reduced phosphorylation of eIF2α and expression of ATF4 and 4F2 (SLC3A2) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B and citation to Novoa et al., 2001

claim: Treatment of LNCaP cells with halofuginone resulted in robust activation of GCN2 and increased expression of ATF4 and 4F2 (SLC3A2) protein and mRNA.
source: Further supporting the central role of activation of GCN2 in the induction of 4F2 (SLC3A2) expression, treatment of LNCaP cells with halofuginone, an inhibitor of EPRS and prolyl-tRNA charging (Keller et al., 2012) resulted in robust activation of GCN2 and increased expression of ATF4 and 4F2 (SLC3A2) protein and mRNA (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, and citation to Keller et al., 2012

claim: Knockdown of 4F2 (SLC3A2) expression using siRNA significantly reduced growth in LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells and led to activation of GCN2 and increased ATF4 protein levels.
source: First, knockdown of 4F2 (SLC3A2) expression using siRNA significantly reduced growth in LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells and led to activation of GCN2 and increased ATF4 protein levels (Figure 4F, G, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by growth assay and immunoblot data shown in Figure 4F, G

claim: Knockdown of 4F2 (SLC3A2) expression did not impact growth of non-cancerous BPH-1 cells.
source: Importantly, knockdown of 4F2 (SLC3A2) expression did not impact growth of non-cancerous BPH-1 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B and Figure 1—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: Supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B and 5C

claim: Overexpression of 4F2 (SLC3A2) rescued the growth defect caused by loss of GCN2 function in LNCaP cells.
source: As was shown earlier, loss of GCN2 function using siRNA or GCN2iB treatment in cultured LNCaP cells reduced growth (Figure 1A, D). This growth defect was rescued by overexpression of 4F2 (SLC3A2) (Figure 4H and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 4H

claim: Overexpression of 4F2 (SLC3A2) reduced GCN2 activity, lowered p-GCN2 and p-eIF2α levels, and reduced ATF4 protein expression in LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells.
source: Importantly, overexpression of 4F2 (SLC3A2) reduced GCN2 activity, which lowered p-GCN2 and p-eIF2α levels, along with ATF4 protein expression, and provided a growth advantage in both wild-type LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot and growth assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C and 3D

claim: Knockdown of SLC3A2 reduced a subset of amino acids as compared to knockdown of GCN2 in LNCaP cells.
source: As anticipated, knockdown of SLC3A2 reduced a subset of amino acids as compared to knockdown of GCN2 (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by amino acid measurements shown in Figure 4I

claim: Parental 22Rv1 cells with functional GCN2 showed sustained tumor growth, while loss of GCN2 significantly reduced tumor growth over time in a mouse xenograft model.
source: Whereas the parental cells showed sustained tumor growth, loss of GCN2 significantly reduced tumor growth over time, resulting in a significant reduction in tumor weight at the end of the study (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 6A

claim: GCN2 KO 22Rv1 tumors showed diminished expression of Ki-67, a marker for cell proliferation.
source: IHC staining of tumor preparations showed diminished expression of Ki-67, a marker for cell proliferation in 22Rv1 tumors devoid of GCN2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: GCN2 protein was not detectable in the GCN2 KO 22Rv1 tumors, p-GCN2-T899 staining was reduced, and expression levels of 4F2 (SLC3A2), xCT (SLC7A11), and LAT1 (SLC7A5) were sharply reduced.
source: As expected, the GCN2 protein was not detectable in the GCN2 KO tumors as judged by immunoblot, p-GCN2-T899 staining was reduced, and expression levels of the GCN2-targeted transporters 4F2 (SLC3A2), xCT (SLC7A11), and LAT1 (SLC7A5) were sharply reduced (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot and IHC data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: 22Rv1 tumors maintained expression of the ARv7 variant.
source: Furthermore, the 22Rv1 tumors maintained expression of the ARv7 variant, which provides for castration resistance and resistance to enzalutamide (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Similar results to 22Rv1 were obtained in the AR-null castration-resistant cell line PC-3 following deletion of GCN2 in a xenograft model.
source: Similar results were obtained in the AR-null castration-resistant cell line PC-3 following deletion of GCN2 (Figure 6C, D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by xenograft tumor growth and immunoblot data shown in Figure 6C, D and supplementary figures

claim: Loss of GCN2 led to dramatically reduced tumor growth in 22Rv1 xenografts, while deletion of ATF4 only delayed tumor growth relative to wild-type parental cells.
source: While loss of GCN2 led to dramatically reduced tumor growth, deletion of ATF4 only delayed tumor growth relative to the wild-type parental cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 6E

claim: Deletion of GCN2 led to a further decrease in 4F2 (SLC3A2), ASCT2 (SLC1A5), and CAT1 (SLC7A1) protein levels as compared to loss of ATF4 in 22Rv1 tumors.
source: Furthermore, deletion of GCN2 led to a further decrease in 4F2 (SLC3A2), ASCT2 (SLC1A5), and CAT1 (SLC7A1) protein levels as compared to loss of ATF4 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A

claim: Loss of GCN2 did not reduce p-eIF2α levels in end stage 22Rv1 tumors.
source: It is noted that loss of GCN2 did not reduce p-eIF2α levels in these end stage tumors, suggesting activation of a secondary eIF2 kinase or reduced phosphatase-directed dephosphorylation of eIF2α, which has been reported earlier in cells during extended nutrient limitation or other stress conditions (Jiang et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and citations to Jiang et al., 2004 and Zhang et al., 2002

claim: Deletion of ATF4 resulted in increased activation of GCN2, increased levels of p-eIF2α, and in some cases increased amino acids relative to GCN2 KO tumors.
source: Interestingly, deletion of ATF4 resulted in increased activation of GCN2, increased levels of p-eIF2α, and in some cases increased amino acids relative to GCN2 KO tumors (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot and amino acid measurement data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A

claim: Consumption of EAA-supplemented water by GCN2 KO-tumor bearing mice provided for increased tumor growth approaching that of wild-type GCN2 tumors.
